questions.knowledgeNote: b*cosC - c*cosB collapses to (b^2-c^2)/a: clear the denominators first.
questions.question: Q1(a). In any triangle, prove that a(b*cosC - c*cosB) = b^2 - c^2.
questions.solution: By the cosine rule cosC = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2ab) and cosB = (a^2-b^2+c^2)/(2ac). So b*cosC - c*cosB = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2a) - (a^2-b^2+c^2)/(2a) = (2b^2-2c^2)/(2a) = (b^2-c^2)/a. Multiplying by a gives a(b*cosC - c*cosB) = b^2 - c^2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(a); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: All three expressions equal the same symmetric value (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc): prove one, the others follow by cyclic symmetry.
questions.question: Q1(b). In any triangle, prove that cosA/a + a/(bc) = cosB/b + b/(ca) = cosC/c + c/(ab).
questions.solution: cosA/a + a/(bc) = (bc*cosA + a^2)/(abc). Since bc*cosA = bc*(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc) = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2, the numerator is (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2 + a^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2. Hence the first expression equals (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc). The second and third are the same computation with cyclically permuted letters, so all three are equal to (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(b); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Put everything over abc and use bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2: the six terms pair up.
questions.question: Q1(c). In any triangle, prove that cosA/a + cosB/b + cosC/c = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.solution: With common denominator abc the left side is (bc*cosA + ca*cosB + ab*cosC)/(abc). Now bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2, ca*cosB = (c^2+a^2-b^2)/2, ab*cosC = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/2, whose sum is (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2. Dividing by abc gives (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(c); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a^3 = 8R^3*sin^3A turns the whole sum into a telescoping sine product.
questions.question: Q2(a). In any triangle, prove that a^3*(sin^3B - sin^3C) + b^3*(sin^3C - sin^3A) + c^3*(sin^3A - sin^3B) = 0.
questions.solution: By the sine rule a = 2R*sinA, so a^3 = 8R^3*sin^3A (and cyclically). The left side becomes 8R^3*[sin^3A*(sin^3B - sin^3C) + sin^3B*(sin^3C - sin^3A) + sin^3C*(sin^3A - sin^3B)] = 8R^3*[sin^3A*sin^3B - sin^3A*sin^3C + sin^3B*sin^3C - sin^3B*sin^3A + sin^3C*sin^3A - sin^3C*sin^3B] = 0, since the six terms cancel in pairs.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(a); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each fraction simplifies to 4R^2*sinA*sin(B-C); the sine-product sum telescopes to zero.
questions.question: Q2(b). In any triangle, prove that [a^2*sin(B-C)]/sinA + [b^2*sin(C-A)]/sinB + [c^2*sin(A-B)]/sinC = 0. (T.U. 2052)
questions.solution: Since a^2 = 4R^2*sin^2A, the first term is 4R^2*sinA*sin(B-C) (and cyclically). Now sinA*sin(B-C) = [cos(A-B+C) - cos(A+B-C)]/2 = [cos(pi-2B) - cos(pi-2C)]/2 = (cos2C - cos2B)/2. Summing cyclically: (1/2)*[(cos2C - cos2B) + (cos2A - cos2C) + (cos2B - cos2A)] = 0. Hence the whole sum is 4R^2*0 = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(b) (T.U. 2052); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each fraction equals the constant 1/(2R), so all three are equal: b^2-c^2 = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA is the key step.
questions.question: Q2(c). In any triangle, prove that [a*sin(B-C)]/(b^2-c^2) = [b*sin(C-A)]/(c^2-a^2) = [c*sin(A-B)]/(a^2-b^2). (T.U. 2051H)
questions.solution: b^2 - c^2 = 4R^2*(sin^2B - sin^2C) = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sin(B+C) = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA. So the first fraction is 2R*sinA*sin(B-C)/[4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA] = 1/(2R). The same computation cyclically gives 1/(2R) for the second and third fractions, so all three are equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(c) (T.U. 2051H); book p186 = PDF p213-214 (vision read)
